..
Issued at 1027 PM CDT Sat Sep 5 2026

Tonight and Sunday...

Water vapor imagery and objective analysis late this evening depicts 
a high amplitude mid-level ridge over the central CONUS, with a 
cutoff low moving onshore over the Pacific Northwest. At the 
surface, high temperature peaked in the low to mid 90s under the 
persistent ridge, approximately 10 degrees above average for early 
September. Dewpoints soared into the low 70s, pushing heat index 
values into the 102-107 degree range. As temperatures cooled through 
the evening, the Heat Advisory was allowed to expire. 

Overnight, convection is expected to develop along a lee trough over 
western Nebraska before gradually progressing eastward along the LLJ 
into the mid to late morning hours. Some questions remains regarding 
storm coverage and intensity as they progress towards the area, 
given the rather unimpressive bulk shear (20 kts). Intermittent CAM 
guidance also sparks more isolated storm development in northeast 
NE/southeast SD overnight along the LLJ nose, though confidence in 
this scenario remains a bit lower given the subtle forcing. However, 
storm coverage is expected to become more widespread through the 
late morning and early afternoon as increasing low-level warm air 
advection noses into a surface front draped near the mid-MO Valley 
as mid-level disturbance pivots over the area. A corridor of 
modestly improved bulk shear around 25 kts will overlap steepening 
lapse rates and modest instability across far eastern Nebraska and 
western Iowa, supporting some potential for strong to severe storms. 

The primary hazards will be pockets of hail and damaging wind gusts 
as individual cores quickly pulse within a broader, more upscale 
cluster. Potential also exists for pockets of heavy rainfall given 
that storms may train over the same for an extended period of time. 
Efficient rainfall processes will be in place with PWAT values of 
1.75-2.00" (above the 90th percentile of sounding climatology for 
early September) and warm cloud depths of 4-4.5 km. CAM guidance 
hints of pockets of 2-4" rainfall totals, particularly over 
northeast Nebraska into western Iowa where convection is more 
persistent. 

Although cloud cover and precipitation chances will increase through 
the day, high temperatures will still make a run at hitting the 
upper 80s and low 90s prior to convection becoming more widespread, 
bringing yet another above-average early September day. Heat index 
values are expected to peak in the 95-100 degree range, just shy of 
Heat Advisory criteria. Precipitation chances will taper off through 
the overnight period into Monday morning. 

Monday and Tuesday...

Into the work week, the aforementioned mid-level low positioned over 
the Pacific Northwest will gradually deepen and pull east along the 
US/Canada border, helping to flatten the ridge in place and push a 
cold front through the area. Long range guidance varies on the exact 
timing of the frontal passage, though it looks to sweep southward 
across the area through the day Tuesday and into early Wednesday. 
Ahead of its arrival, Monday will be yet another day of widespread 
highs in the upper 80s to mid 90s, with heat index values around 
100. A tightening surface pressure gradient ahead of the approaching 
system and mixing into stronger winds aloft will bring southerly 
wind gusts of 25-35+ mph on Monday. 

High temperatures on Tuesday will depend on how quick the northeast-
to-southwest oriented cold front pushes southward across the area. 
Highs are expected to reach the mid to upper 90s, with heat index 
values around 105, across southeast NE and southwest IA, with values 
peaking in the upper 80s further north where the front passes 
through before peak daytime heating. Chances for showers and storms 
exist along the front, with machine learning guidance placing a 5-
15% probability of severe weather. With the better large-scale 
forcing for ascent displaced to the northeast, details will likely 
hinge on mesoscale features that come into focus with time, though 
sufficient instability and improved bulk shear will be in place for 
a few stronger storms. For now, PoPs of 60-80% exist through Tuesday 
and early Wednesday as the front pushes through. 

Wednesday and Beyond...

Zonal flow aloft will return by mid-week, pushing high temperatures 
back into the 80s. Periodic PoPs of 15-30% remain in place through 
the remainder of the week as shortwave disturbance traverse the 
area. Good news for the fall-lovers, looking further ahead, most 
GEFS and EPS-AIFS members bring a potent trough across the northern 
Plains next weekend. This system will bring a push of cooler air 
into the region and could knock highs in the 70s by the end of next 
weekend, though details on timing and extent will still need to be 
ironed out.
